B00_00: This concerns exchange between the cytoplasm and the nucleus in human cells, which supports nuclear signalling that influences gene regulation, messenger export and release of stored ions at the nuclear envelope. Its integrity sets the conditions for that nuclear signalling. Defects in the nuclear pore broadly disturb nucleocytoplasmic exchange, as in triple A syndrome, an inherited disorder of adrenal insufficiency, absent tears and failure of the oesophagus to relax.
B00_01: Parasympathetic nerve input to the pancreatic islets boosts hormone release from beta cells during a meal, explaining why eating produces a larger secretory response than the same sugar load given into a vein. The boost operates only when blood sugar is already elevated, so the nerve amplifies rather than initiates secretion, and loss of this vagal control blunts the early phase of the response.
B00_02: Endothelial cells lining blood vessels produce a signal that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, limits platelet adhesion and leukocyte recruitment, and sets basal blood pressure. Switching this output on is central to vascular health. Its loss is a defining feature of endothelial dysfunction in hypertension, atherosclerosis and diabetes, where vessels fail to relax and the vessel wall becomes inflamed and prone to thrombosis.
B00_03: During stress and exercise, sympathetic nerves and adrenal stress hormones suppress hormone release from pancreatic beta cells so that blood sugar stays available to working tissues. This brake opposes the normal sugar-triggered secretion of the islets. Inherited variation affecting it has been linked to impaired beta-cell secretion and type 2 diabetes risk, and drugs acting on this adrenergic route pharmacologically suppress pancreatic hormone output.
B00_04: Every cell must keep balanced supplies of the building blocks used for transcription, DNA replication, repair and energy metabolism, a demand that is greatest in proliferating tissue. When these supplies become unbalanced, cells suffer replication stress and increased mutation. In mitochondria the result can be depletion of mitochondrial DNA, a cause of inherited mitochondrial disease affecting muscle, liver and brain.
B00_05: These signals act as cellular sensors of energy and phosphate status in mammals, tuning pancreatic hormone secretion and responsiveness, systemic phosphate homeostasis, vesicle trafficking, telomere length and the response to DNA damage. Their relevance therefore spans metabolic disease and genome maintenance. In mice, loss of a key producing enzyme impairs growth, fertility and metabolic hormone signalling, underlining their physiological importance.
B00_06: In liver and adipose tissue, high dietary sugar is turned into a signal that drives conversion of surplus carbohydrate into fat. This nutrient-sensing response complements hormonal control of fat synthesis in the fed state. Its overactivity contributes to fatty liver (hepatic steatosis) and abnormal blood lipid levels (dyslipidaemia), linking excessive carbohydrate intake to metabolic disease.
B00_07: Pancreatic beta cells secrete more of their blood-sugar-lowering hormone when circulating dietary fats accompany a rise in blood sugar. This lipid-sensing arm of nutrient-stimulated secretion links circulating fat to glycaemic control. It has been pursued as a drug target in type 2 diabetes because it enhances secretion only when blood sugar is high, and it bears on how chronic fat exposure alters beta-cell function.
B00_08: This concerns building a central component of the mitochondrial energy-producing machinery in human cells. When it fails, cellular respiration stalls and patients develop a mitochondrial disorder presenting in infancy with encephalopathy, liver failure, kidney tubule dysfunction and lactic acidosis. Defects in the mitochondrial supply of required cofactors, as in Friedreich ataxia, feed into the same process.
B00_09: Recycling building blocks from degraded nucleic acids keeps nucleotide supplies balanced at low energetic cost and is the main supply route in tissues with limited synthetic capacity and in mitochondria. Its loss in mitochondria causes mitochondrial DNA depletion with myopathy. Because the same process activates and clears nucleoside-analogue drugs, it shapes patient responses to chemotherapy and antiviral treatment.
B00_10: This concerns building the entry point of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, which supplies most of the energy used by human cells, especially in brain, muscle and eye. Defects in its many components or assembly helpers cause isolated respiratory chain deficiency, a frequent inherited mitochondrial energy disorder, presenting as Leigh syndrome, encephalomyopathy and optic neuropathy, often in infancy or childhood.
B00_11: Almost all of the energy that human cells spend is produced at this final step of mitochondrial energy conversion, so every tissue depends on it. Inherited defects cause a mitochondrial disorder presenting with encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy. When the mitochondrial membrane potential collapses, as in oxygen deprivation, the same machinery can run in reverse and drain the cell's energy reserves.
B00_12: Making purine building blocks from scratch supplies DNA and RNA precursors and energy carriers, and demand rises sharply in proliferating tissue such as activated lymphocytes and tumours. That is why drugs blocking this route suppress immune cell expansion and why antifolate drugs cripple cell division. Inherited deficiency of one step causes a neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and autistic features.
B00_13: This committed mitochondrial step links sugar breakdown to aerobic energy production, and the brain depends heavily on it. When it fails, sugar-derived fuel cannot be burned aerobically, and patients present with congenital lactic acidosis, encephalopathy and Leigh-like neurodegeneration, typically in infancy or childhood. It is among the more frequent inherited causes of lactic acidosis in children.
B00_14: Outside cells, nucleotides released by damaged or activated cells act as signals, and how long they persist shapes platelet aggregation and haemostasis, inflammatory and immune responses, and neurotransmission and nervous system development. The relevant activity is found on blood vessel lining and on regulatory T cells, among other sites, making it important for vascular protection, immune suppression and neural function.
B00_15: Many tissues, especially brain, heart and liver, must transfer reducing power from the cytosol into mitochondria to keep sugar breakdown running and to supply certain amino acids. Loss of this shuttle in the brain presents as early infantile epileptic encephalopathy. Defects in one of its carriers cause a liver disorder with neonatal cholestasis and hyperammonaemia, also seen in adults with recurrent encephalopathy.
B00_16: When dietary sugar is abundant, liver and adipose tissue convert the surplus into fat for storage, coupling the fed state to fat synthesis. This transcriptional programme acts alongside hormonal control after meals. Its overactivity contributes to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridaemia, whereas its loss impairs the storage of dietary carbohydrate as fat, linking it to metabolic liver disease.
B00_17: After a meal, hormonal signals in liver and adipose tissue redirect sugar metabolism toward nucleotide synthesis, biosynthesis and fat production, forming a feed-forward loop linking the fed state to sugar breakdown and lipogenic gene expression. This arm depends on a vitamin-derived cofactor, which is why it falters in vitamin deficiency states such as beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy, seen in malnutrition and alcoholism.
B00_18: Circulating lipid-derived signals secreted into the blood raise whole-body energy expenditure by making mitochondria burn fuel less efficiently, independently of classical brown-fat thermogenesis. In mice, higher levels of these signals accompany increased energy expenditure and better blood sugar handling. This places the process alongside brown-fat heat production and makes it of interest for treating obesity and metabolic disease.
B00_19: Proliferating cells depend on making pyrimidine building blocks from scratch to keep pace with DNA replication and RNA synthesis, which is why this process is a drug target in cancer, autoimmune disease and antiparasitic therapy. Its coupling to mitochondrial respiration ties it to cellular energy status. Inherited loss of the final step causes a hereditary disorder with megaloblastic anaemia and abnormal urinary excretion.
B00_20: Recycling purine building blocks from nucleic acid turnover is energetically cheap and matters most where synthesis from scratch is weak, such as in brain and lymphocytes. One defect causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, with hyperuricaemia and severe neurological disease, while another poisons lymphocytes and produces severe combined immunodeficiency. The process also activates certain nucleoside analogue drugs and influences gout risk.
B00_21: In brown adipose tissue, mitochondria can release energy as heat rather than storing it, the basis of non-shivering thermogenesis recruited when mammals are exposed to cold. This capacity is of interest for energy balance and obesity treatment. Related carriers expressed far more widely, including in brain and kidney, are linked to control of oxidative stress and fat handling rather than heat production.
B00_22: Regulating this mitochondrial gateway decides whether tissues burn sugar or conserve it: switching it off spares sugar during fasting and shifts muscle and other tissues onto fat oxidation, while keeping it on feeds sugar into energy production and fat synthesis after meals. Inherited defects cause lactic acidosis and neurological disease, and persistent switching-off underlies the fermentative metabolism of many tumours.
B00_23: Highly charged signalling molecules that act inside the nucleus to influence chromatin, messenger export and transcription must move between cytosol and nucleus in human cells rather than being made only where they are used. This exchange across the nuclear envelope supports nuclear signalling in gene regulation. Because the transport mechanism is not established, the process is best viewed as a conduit between compartments.
B00_24: Mitochondria in human cells must clear a metabolic dead-end product so its carbon can be reused for energy production. Inherited loss of either of two clearing activities causes one of two related organic acidurias, with variable encephalopathy, seizures and developmental delay. The process also matters in cancer, where accumulation of the same product disturbs epigenetic regulation of DNA and chromatin.
B00_25: Several small signals that regulate cellular signalling, phosphate sensing and vesicle traffic are made in the nucleus and must reach the cytosol to act, so their movement keeps nuclear production coupled to cytoplasmic signalling in human cells. The underlying transport is not well defined and is treated as passive passage across the nuclear envelope rather than as dedicated, carrier-mediated transport.
B00_26: Endothelial cells tune their output of a vessel-relaxing signal by relocating its source away from the plasma membrane. Because this endothelial signal controls vessel tone, platelet adhesion and vascular permeability, the relocation adjusts blood vessel relaxation. Its dysregulation belongs to the broader picture of endothelial dysfunction in hypertension and atherosclerosis, linking vascular signalling to membrane internalisation in the endothelium.
B00_27: Within the endoplasmic reticulum of human cells, a set of signalling and phosphate-storage molecules is trimmed, shaping the pool available when membranes are disrupted and influencing cell signalling and phosphate handling. Its importance is shown in humans: loss of this activity causes a severe pontocerebellar hypoplasia, linking it to brain development, particularly of the cerebellum and brainstem.
B00_28: Cells must keep their nucleotide supplies free of damaged or surplus species that would otherwise be built into DNA as mutations or into messenger RNA as faulty protein. This sanitation protects genome integrity and protein quality. It also sets patient tolerance to certain anticancer and immunosuppressive drugs, and inherited variants cause severe drug toxicity, notably bone marrow suppression.
B00_29: The incretin effect, in which an eaten sugar load releases far more pancreatic hormone than the same load given intravenously, depends on a gut-derived hormone from intestinal cells acting on pancreatic beta cells. It is the target of widely used type 2 diabetes drugs, and because its effect requires raised blood sugar, it boosts secretion without causing hypoglycaemia. It also supports beta-cell mass.
B00_30: This concerns building the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, which consumes oxygen to support energy production in every tissue. Tissue-specific and low-oxygen-responsive versions tune it to local needs. Inherited defects in any of its many components or assembly helpers cause a respiratory chain deficiency, typically presenting as Leigh syndrome and other infantile encephalomyopathies.
B00_31: When cellular energy falls, the liver stops converting sugar into fat, conserving fuel while energy is scarce. A hormone released from fat tissue reinforces this restraint, linking adipose signalling to liver metabolism. Loss of the restraint contributes to fatty liver and the abnormal blood lipids of insulin resistance, which is why this energy-sensing route and fat-derived hormone signalling are pursued as metabolic drug targets.
B00_32: Endothelial cells lining blood vessels adjust their production of a vessel-relaxing signal by moving its source away from the cell surface. Since this signal relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelet aggregation and limits leukocyte adhesion, the relocation tunes vascular tone and blood pressure. Because it varies with cell cycle stage, it links endothelial proliferation to vascular signalling output.
B00_33: This rate-limiting step of mitochondrial energy metabolism sets how much fuel feeds respiration and how much nitrogen handling mitochondria can support, particularly in brain and other energy-demanding tissues. It is a notable source of mitochondrial oxidative stress. Inherited loss causes encephalopathy and lactic acidosis, and its impairment is associated with tumour-related metabolic disturbances.
B00_34: Within the nucleus of human cells, a family of soluble signals couples phosphate and energy status to gene expression, messenger export, DNA repair and programmed cell death, and shapes how cells sense and store phosphate. Loss of individual producing steps alters growth signalling and stress responses, and the same activity influences pancreatic hormone secretion and tumour cell survival, linking nuclear signalling to metabolism.
B00_35: Many hormones, neurotransmitters, growth factors and immune stimuli trigger second-messenger signals in cells, and this process sets how long such signals last and what they become, influencing secretion, membrane trafficking and immune activation. Its importance is clinical: loss of one terminating activity causes Lowe syndrome, affecting eyes, brain and kidneys, and another shapes immune cell activation thresholds.
B00_36: After receptor stimulation, cells must recover a precursor needed to rebuild signalling lipids, terminating second-messenger and growth-factor signals while replenishing supplies. Defects cause Lowe oculocerebrorenal syndrome, impair synaptic vesicle recycling in neurons, and remove a tumour suppressor. Inhibition by a mood-stabilising drug used in bipolar disorder places this recycling route at the centre of mood-disorder pharmacology.
B00_37: Pancreatic beta cells release more of their hormone when circulating fats are available, partly because burning dietary fat raises the cell's energy state. This links circulating lipid supply to hormone output after meals. Chronic fat excess distorts the response, contributing to beta-cell lipotoxicity and the secretory failure of type 2 diabetes, tying whole-body lipid handling to blood sugar control.
B00_38: Mitochondria must prepare and regulate the enzymes of their central energy-generating cycle before it can run, setting how much oxidative energy metabolism cells can support according to nutrient state. Defects in this preparatory layer cause inherited mitochondrial disease, hereditary paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma tumours, and Friedreich ataxia, a neurodegenerative disorder with cardiomyopathy.
B00_39: When fasting or stress hormones rise, liver and muscle switch from storing sugar to mobilising stored carbohydrate and, in liver, exporting sugar into the blood. Without this switch, tissues could not respond to fasting or stress. It acts both acutely and through longer-term control of genes for sugar breakdown and fat synthesis, linking hormonal signals to whole-body fuel balance.
B00_40: The body disposes of nucleic acid building blocks released from nucleotide turnover and dietary sources, excreting the products in urine. The process matters clinically because it also clears a widely used class of cancer chemotherapy drugs: inherited deficiency causes severe, sometimes fatal drug toxicity. Inherited defects at each step also produce neurological disease, and its products can feed amino acid and fat metabolism.
B00_41: When blood sugar falls, a pancreatic hormone acts on liver cells to mobilise stored fuel, driving breakdown of stored carbohydrate, new sugar production and fat breakdown. Different tissues tune the size of the response. Disturbances upset blood sugar homeostasis, and overactivating mutations or loss of a restraining component cause endocrine tumour syndromes such as McCune-Albright syndrome and Carney complex.
